title: Hemichorea-Hemiballism in A 50-Year-Old Man With Newly Diagnosed Diabetes
case_prompt:
A 50-year-old man presented with 20 days of persistent, involuntary movements of the right arm and leg that ceased only during sleep and severely impaired his daily activities. One month earlier, he had developed polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss and was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, for which he was prescribed metformin and glimepiride but proved poorly compliant.

On examination, he was alert and cooperative but undernourished. He had nonrhythmic, jerky, flailing movements of the right upper and lower limbs consistent with hemichorea with a ballistic component. Vital signs were: pulse 90 /min regular, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, random capillary glucose 18 mmol/L. Higher functions and cranial nerves were normal. There was no tremor, rigidity, cerebellar signs, or sensory deficits. Muscle strength and reflexes were normal; gait was unstable. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin A1C 15.1% (141.5 mmol/mol), fasting glucose 14.2 mmol/L, postprandial glucose 19.1 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, ESR 21 mm/h, normal leukocyte and platelet counts. Urinalysis demonstrated sugar (++), no albumin, and no ketones. Serum creatinine and electrolytes were within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the head was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated a T1 hyperintense lesion in the left caudate and lentiform nuclei that was iso- to hyperintense on T2/FLAIR, with no diffusion restriction and no enhancement after contrast administration.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke was considered — “Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke represents the most common cause” … “Computed tomography scan of the brain was unremarkable, but MRI … There was no restriction of diffusion on the diffusion-weighted image.”  
2. Hyperglycemia-induced HCHB was considered — “hyperglycemia is the second most common cause” … “random capillary blood glucose level was 18 mmol/L” and “His hemoglobin A1C level was 15.1% (141.5 mmol/mol).”  
3. Diabetic ketoacidosis–associated HCHB was considered — “an association with diabetic ketoacidosis has also been reported” … “ketone–absent.”  
4. Encephalitis was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause of HCHB in our patient, and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”  
5. Vasculitis was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause … and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”  
6. CNS lupus was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause … and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”  
7. Mass lesions were considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “no remarkable enhancement after intravenous contrast.”  
8. Multiple sclerosis was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause … and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”  
9. Thyrotoxicosis was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs…” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause … and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”

Drug-induced movement disorder was considered — “Rarer causes include encephalitis, vasculitis, CNS lupus, mass lesions, multiple sclerosis, thyrotoxicosis, and drugs (ie, anticonvulsants, levodopa, oral contraceptives, and neuroleptics)” … “Hyperglycemia was the underlying cause … and the presentation makes other diagnoses unlikely.”
